title: Capacity, energy and source equations
scope: The nonlinear branch fixes the original valued field, the full original test sheaf, one allowed symmetric middle-positive separately closed background S of degree (p,p), and a strict Laurent domain whose closure lies in an affinoid interior and to whose neighborhood S extends. Write q=n−p≥1 and d=q+1. Completed potentials are relative Borel classes, not automatically ambient classical psh functions. The q=1 Dirichlet branch uses its own faithful part-energy space and energy capacity. Known means established in the cited source, with no new independent proof acceptance.

nodes.title: Capacity tails and truncation calculus
nodes.summary: In the stated zero-boundary class, no loss is equivalent to t^q C_S({u<−t})→0, and finite σ-energy is equivalent to the weighted capacity integral J_σ(u)<∞. Bounded capacity completion and graded truncation bounds then control curvature, first-order and energy coefficients. Local finiteness is required for the nonpolar product; restricted truncation stages need not be closed.

links.label: Theorem 7.2: capacity and truncation estimates
Definition 7.1: actual power-energy classes

nodes.title: Bounded global Green exchange
nodes.summary: For bounded negative classical potentials with compact negative sublevels and finite total curvature masses, Green exchange identifies the two weighted curvature integrals with the integrated cross-energy. This supplies the exchange of the undifferentiated slot needed for global mixed energy.

links.label: Lemma 7.3 and proof: global Green exchange

nodes.title: Symmetric mixed energy and Hölder
nodes.summary: For actual first-energy potentials, B(u₀,…,u_q) is finite and symmetric in every slot. Positive energy matrices give Cauchy–Schwarz, the mixed Hölder inequality has constant one, and the energy root satisfies Minkowski. The associated tester and sharp midpoint estimates control strong discrepancy.

links.label: Theorem 7.4 and proof: first mixed energy
Theorem 7.5: uniform energy testing
Proposition 7.6: sharp midpoint bound

nodes.title: Complete relative first-energy space
nodes.summary: Strongly Cauchy rows have uniform deep tails and global weighted tightness. Their relative Borel limits carry intrinsic currents and critical weighted limits. The completed cone C is complete, with strong convergence exactly equivalent to local truncated outer-capacity convergence together with energy convergence. A common lower barrier is not required for a Cauchy row.

links.label: Lemma 8.1: uniform tails and tightness
Theorem 8.4: completed critical calculus
Theorem 8.6: completeness and the topology equivalence

nodes.title: Banach differences and closed sources
nodes.summary: The actual Borel difference space D_S=C−C is Banach. The curvature functional J(u)(h)=B(h,u,…,u) is injective; its image is norm closed, and the dual distance between sources gives a complete metric inducing the strong topology on C. Closed image does not assert surjectivity onto the dual.

links.label: Theorem 9.3 and proof: Banach realization
Theorem 9.6 and proof: closed source image

nodes.title: Literal, strongly continuous datum
nodes.summary: The positive Radon measure μ defines ℓ_μ(h)=−∫h dμ literally on every Borel difference in D_S: absolute integrability, independence of relative-null representatives, norm boundedness and strong continuity on C are all required. Fixed completed-source domination is one proved sufficient condition. Norm boundedness alone is the open ED-STRONG question.

links.label: Definition 9.7: the strong-continuous dual
Fixed domination theorem and proof
Question 6.1: literal strong continuity

nodes.title: Projection and a normal residual
nodes.summary: For a strongly continuous dual datum, maximizing ℓ(v)−e(v)/(q+1) on C gives a unique u=Π(ℓ). Its decomposition ℓ=J(u)+n satisfies n(v)≤0 on C and n(u)=0. The source equation still requires the residual to vanish in the appropriate literal sense.

links.label: Theorem 9.9 and proof: variational normal decomposition
Theorem 9.10: source retraction and residual gap

nodes.title: One probe with both test directions
nodes.summary: The strict Laurent geometry supplies a single bounded continuous negative classical ψ₀. For every original compact smooth scalar φ, both ψ₀+ε_φφ and ψ₀−ε_φφ lie in the actual first-energy cone for some ε_φ>0. The same probe works for every extending allowed background.

links.label: Lemma 9.11: exact moment compensators
Proposition 9.12 and proof: the simultaneous probe

nodes.title: Additional compatibility: Ξ=0
nodes.summary: For the normal pair of a literal strongly continuous positive datum, Ξ=J(Πℓ_μ)(ψ₀)−ℓ_μ(ψ₀)=−n(ψ₀) is nonnegative. Requiring Ξ=0 is the extra compatibility condition. Strong continuity and fixed-source domination do not force this equality.

links.label: Theorem 9.13: the scalar source defect

nodes.title: Unique source solution in the completed cone
nodes.summary: Under the literal strong-dual hypotheses, Ξ=0 if and only if μ̂_{Πℓ_μ}=μ, if and only if some v∈C has source μ. Any solution equals Πℓ_μ. More generally, every compact original test error is bounded by ε_φ⁻¹Ξ. This is an exact compatibility criterion, not an assertion that arbitrary data are compatible.

links.label: Theorem 9.13 and proof: all three equivalent conditions

nodes.title: Smooth dominated data can have Ξ>0
nodes.summary: In a fixed two-dimensional torus model with q=1, smooth positive densities f_j→1 uniformly can make f_jμ_w leave the entire strong-completion source image, even at a fixed reference admitting every two-sided compact test direction. These data remain literal, strongly continuous and uniformly source dominated. Their zero-boundary Poisson traces fail convexity.

links.label: Fixed-source counterexample: theorem and proof
Programme: the smooth-density obstruction

nodes.title: Find source conditions from the data
nodes.summary: Find substantial geometric classes of given μ for which strong continuity and Ξ=0 follow from checkable input conditions. A local inverse route needs a specified linearized range, a right inverse with boundary and moment estimates, and preservation of that range by the nonlinear remainder. Assuming an unknown solution would restate the goal.

links.label: Problem 6.3: compatible source classes
The proposed linearization and its missing range control

nodes.title: q=1, faithful part form, diffuse data
nodes.summary: Take remaining degree q=1, V compactly contained in an ordinary neighborhood inside an affinoid interior, and an allowed background S there. Use the faithful regular strongly local coercive part form of the original smooth core. The datum is finite signed Radon on V∩supp S, with total variation annihilating energy-capacity polar sets.

links.label: Section 10: domain and faithful-form hypotheses
The original coercive energy form

nodes.title: Renormalized linear Dirichlet solution
nodes.summary: Every such finite signed diffuse datum has a unique zero-boundary renormalized solution of D(uS)=μ. Its clippings lie in the part-energy space H; chain, radiation and stability identities hold on the original tests. The solution need not belong to the classical psh cone or the nonlinear strong first-energy cone C.

links.label: Theorem 10.1 and proof: transposition
Theorem 10.9 and proof: unique renormalized solution
Theorem 10.10: strong clipping stability

nodes.title: Extend domains and recover representatives
nodes.summary: Beyond strict Laurent domains, establish barriers, Green exchange, cutoff control and weighted boundary tightness under explicit geometric assumptions. Separately identify subclasses of completed Borel potentials with canonical ambient classical psh representatives, using a proved regularization or detection theorem rather than identifying different quotients by definition.

links.label: Problem 7.1: domains and boundary control
Problem 7.2: classical representatives

nodes.title: Relative singularity invariants
nodes.summary: For explicit potential and background classes, determine which nonpolar masses, no-loss conditions and energy integrability properties survive bounded changes of singularity. Construct the corresponding envelopes and comparison results with specified domains, boundaries and relative null ideals, and study only modifications for which the required current operations are defined.

links.label: Problem 7.3: relative singularity invariants

nodes.title: Finite-energy Green products
nodes.summary: Define integrable truncation products for Green currents Dg_Z+δ_Z=ω_Z, with presentation independence, symmetry and comparison to existing smooth, formal and delta-form products. Products involving cycle currents require proper-intersection or replacement hypotheses and their own integrability argument.

links.label: Problem 7.4: finite-energy Green products

nodes.title: Adelic finite-energy intersection
nodes.summary: Extend the specified continuous local Chern intersections to finite-energy metrics, then prove placewise summability, boundary control and approximation independence for a global pairing compatible with the product formula. Variation, projection and positivity require their stated global geometric hypotheses.

links.label: Problem 7.5: local and global conditions
Existing continuous local measure input and its scope

nodes.title: Bounded scalar chain calculus
nodes.summary: For a bounded difference f=a−b of actual classical psh functions and a positive separately closed tail current Q, Γ_Q(f) is a positive coefficient-Radon current and smooth scalar compositions satisfy the full original current chain rule. All multipliers are the actual Borel functions.

links.label: LC1–LC2: bounded-difference chain rule and proof

nodes.title: Positive levels, coarea and Stieltjes curvature
nodes.summary: The strict and weak level currents of f are positive and carried by the actual level {f=t}; they need not be closed. Coarea integrates them to Γ_Q(f), and a convex scalar function has a Stieltjes curvature formula retaining every corner atom. Uniform mixed-tail estimates give ordinary-open outer control for the energy capacity attached to f. This energy capacity is distinct from full BT capacity.

links.label: LC4–LC6: positive level currents and their closedness defect
LC7–LC9: coarea on all original tests
SC3: Stieltjes curvature with corner atoms
EC4–EC8: uniform and outer energy-coarea bounds

nodes.title: All-power representatives of prescribed complete poles
nodes.summary: If an actual negative classical u has compact strict negative sublevels on the stated Laurent domain, logarithmic attenuation and barrier gluing produce a potential with exactly the same poles, canonical no loss, finite global top mass and every positive power energy. The representative has exponential capacity tails and can match −log(1−u)−ε near a prescribed compact set. This does not identify every polar set with a complete pole set.

links.label: LP1–LP6: logarithmic attenuation produces no loss
LP7–LP10: all-power representatives and exponential tails

nodes.title: Exact original radial-shell calibration
nodes.summary: On the original q-dimensional unit polydisc with S=[V], g_T=−min(t,T), t=−log max_i|T_i|, has bounded top current δ_{σ(T)}. Scaling gives explicit energy and capacity formulas. As T tends to infinity, the Gauss points σ(T) tend to the rational origin on all original compact scalar tests.

links.label: PS5–PS7: the exact critical-continuity counterexample
CR1–CR4: the logarithmic polar residue

nodes.title: Critical limits need more than bounded energy
nodes.summary: The normalized shell potentials have e_s=1 and converge to zero in full local truncated capacity, while their critical weighted currents converge to the Dirac mass at the origin. Separately, the logarithmic pole has an integrable lower-current multiplier but D(uN_{q−1})=δ_o and nonpolar top product zero. Thus same-power bounds do not replace strong or uniform-tail control, and multiplier integrability does not replace no loss.

links.label: PS5–PS7: the exact critical-continuity counterexample
CR1–CR4: the logarithmic polar residue

nodes.title: Relative Perron envelopes and obstacle projection
nodes.summary: A nonempty family in the completed cone has a relative least upper bound selected by an increasing sequence of finite maxima. Borel upper bounds and a common lower source inequality pass to this envelope. This constructs the greatest cone minorant P(f) for every f∈D_S, with energy-root and curvature estimates. The construction is relative; it supplies neither ambient upper-semicontinuous regularization nor automatic contact orthogonality.

links.label: SE1–SE6: the relative completed Perron theorem
OC2–OC6: the global relative obstacle projection
OC15–OC17: the additional first-order contact gate

nodes.title: Unique constrained barrier maximizer
nodes.summary: For a fixed actual first-energy lower barrier a and finite positive Radon μ that ignores relative outer-capacity null sets and integrates −a, the completed interval [a,0] has a unique maximizer of the functional −e(v)/(q+1)−∫v dμ. Its Euler variational inequality characterizes maximality. The inequality does not assert the unrestricted source equation.

links.label: Completed barrier maximizer: theorem and proof

nodes.title: Coefficient-one rooftop energy fails
nodes.summary: In a two-dimensional original torus with q=1, explicit bounded actual obstacles and one smooth strongly positive background violate e(P(U,V))≤e(U)+e(V). The uniform binary coefficient 2 is sharp across the specified background class. This does not make 2 sharp for every fixed S and does not refute literal strong continuity or mixed-energy Hölder constant one.

links.label: Exact smooth counterexample to coefficient-one rooftop energy
Sharp universal coefficient 2: precise scope

nodes.title: Dual and weak-compactness shortcuts fail
nodes.summary: In the specified smooth torus model with 1≤q<r, canonical convex-trace evaluation is strongly continuous but is not literal integration on relative Borel classes. Literal positive data can converge in dual norm to this nonliteral functional when domination constants are not uniform. In a different radial-mixture background with n>q, an energy-bounded strongly convergent row has no Banach-weak convergent subnet. These examples preserve the fixed-domination closure theorem and closedness of the source image.

links.label: NF7–NF11: a strongly continuous nonliteral positive dual
NF12: literal positive data need not be norm closed
WB1–WB7: no weak cluster and nonreflexivity

nodes.title: A separate parameter L^(k+1) cone
nodes.summary: For an explicitly conormal background R and an actual parameter map s, the new potentials h_c=ψc(s) form a complete L^(k+1)_+(θ) cone, θ=s_*((-ψ)(Dψ)^k∧R). Their mixed currents and energies have exact coefficient-product formulas. This is a new parameter completion with its own boundary interpretation; it is not an identification with the full ambient classical or strong cone.

links.label: PD7–PD10: the new parameter L^d calculus

nodes.title: Exact parameter inverse and energy capacity
nodes.summary: For b≥0 in L^((k+1)/k)(θ), h=ψb(s)^(1/k) solves μ_h=b(s)(Dψ)^k∧R uniquely within the parameter cone. Its energy-normalized capacity equals the L^(k+1)(θ) norm of the conditional source density, has local regularity, and has the null ideal of its fixed source measure. The tester family is explicitly different from full classical [0,1] testers.

links.label: PD12–PD15: the exact parameter source inverse
PC4–PC7: the exact energy-normalized capacity
PC8–PC12: regularity of this parameter capacity

nodes.title: A compatible radial-flux inverse
nodes.summary: For the fixed radial-mixture background of (PO3), nonnegative data with open tail H_ν(t) and nonincreasing e^tH_ν(t) admit the explicit slope A=(e^tH_ν)^(1/q), provided the stated weighted energy integral is finite. The resulting actual potential has no loss and solves the full original source equation. It is unique in the full completed cone; the necessity of the flux condition is asserted for the radial class.

links.label: RF5–RF7: the exact radial-flux inverse
RF13–RF14: the finite-mass radial compatibility condition

nodes.title: Countable Radon probes miss full capacity
nodes.summary: For the allowed coordinate-subtorus background R=[Y] in every n≥q≥1, uncountably many Gauss singletons have uniformly positive full tester capacity. Any countable family of Radon measures misses at least one such singleton. Parameter energy capacities therefore cannot be substituted for full BT capacity. This does not obstruct the single geometry probe for normal defects, test-stage cofinality, or Choquet regularity.

links.label: CM1–CM8: countable Radon probes miss positive-capacity points
CM9: strict separation from the parameter capacity

nodes.title: Complemented clamped linear range
nodes.summary: On a real ball, a bounded right inverse E of normal trace gives P=I−ET from the zero-Dirichlet C^(2,α) space to functions with both boundary traces zero. The Dirichlet inverse yields K and the projection Π onto the clamped Laplacian range. Its complement Q is harmonic, and all harmonic moments characterize the linear range. The infinite-dimensional range condition is explicit.

links.label: The bounded clamped projection and its harmonic-moment range

nodes.title: A small clamped nonlinear source graph
nodes.summary: For the fixed torus background S=β^(n−q)[X], 2≤q≤n, and a protected quadratic reference, the contraction h=C₁⁻¹K(g−N(h)) gives small source data f=g+QN(h(g)). The exact local condition is Qf=QN(h(Πf)). Zero extension adds no sphere mass because both traces vanish. The resulting bounded actual potentials satisfy the source identity on every original test, with a separate negativity budget.

links.label: Contraction construction of the exact clamped source graph
Checked transfer to every original source test

nodes.title: A bulk-and-sphere source graph
nodes.summary: For a specified strictly convex reference, small bulk parameters and a prescribed nonpositive C^(1,α) normal trace produce actual source data with an explicit positive sphere term. The density is ∫_ψ^0 σ_(q−1)(A_T+(s/R)I_T) ds. A quadratic reference also permits explicit inversion of a small nonnegative sphere density. General C^(2,α) references permit prescribed trace; the stronger surface-density regularity is not automatic. A fixed interface admits a common enlarged additive ideal.

links.label: The full bulk-plus-sphere source formula
Reviewed nonradial interface and surface-regularity scope
A common additive ideal for the fixed-interface graph

nodes.title: Moving interfaces separate the topologies
nodes.summary: With q=1 in a fixed smooth torus background and n≥2, moving-sphere potentials converge uniformly and strongly while distinct radii remain separated in the full energy-difference norm. They yield an energy-difference-bounded positive cone functional that is neither strong-continuous nor literal Radon integration. An uncountable family of sphere interfaces also admits no single common principal ideal. None is a counterexample for literal positive Radon data.

links.label: T3–T4: strong convergence with an energy-difference norm gap
T5–T6: the nonliteral, non-strong-continuous dual
Uncountably moving interfaces have no common principal ideal

hypotheses: Fix the original field and tests, the strict Laurent domain, and one allowed S extending to a neighborhood of its closure; q=n−p≥1.
Every input u_i is an actual negative classical first-energy potential with compact negative sublevels, canonical no loss and finite first energy.
Use the Laurent barrier approximants max(u_i,jρ), their finite mixed masses, and the critical weighted convergence supplied by the truncation theorem.
relations.explanation: The proof applies bounded Green exchange after fixing the other curvature slots, then passes the barrier approximants to obtain full mixed symmetry. The positive energy matrix gives Cauchy–Schwarz and Hölder constant one. Repeated slot exchange gives the tester estimate; the segment second-variation formula gives the midpoint bound. These are joint proof inputs, not a claim that a tail bound alone yields global symmetry.

links.label: Theorem 7.4, proof steps 1–3
Lemma 7.3: bounded Green input
Theorem 7.5 and proof: quantitative tester estimate
Proposition 7.6 and proof: midpoint estimate

hypotheses: Retain the same strict Laurent domain and extending background, and actual first-energy approximating rows.
For constructing an unbounded limit, each defining row must be strongly Cauchy: sup_{j,l≥N} I(u_j,u_l)→0.
Use bounded capacity completion at every fixed clipping level and the uniform tester/discrepancy estimates; legal weighted currents satisfy a+b≤q+1.
relations.explanation: Strong Cauchy control, tested against a late fixed row member, gives uniform deep tails and global weighted tightness. Fixed-level capacity limits and vanishing tails define the unbounded coefficients before differentiation. Uniform discrepancy continuity then gives completeness. Energy boundedness plus capacity convergence alone does not supply the critical tail step.

links.label: Lemma 8.1 and proof: Cauchy control produces tails and tightness
Theorem 8.4 and proof: bounded stages to critical currents
Theorem 8.6 and proof: completeness

hypotheses: Form actual Borel differences of the same completed cone C modulo its relative outer-capacity null ideal.
Use the energy-difference norm inf{e(a)^(1/d)+e(b)^(1/d): h=a−b}, completed mixed multilinearity and monotone closure.
Use the exact curvature norm and the two quantitative comparisons between I(u,v) and ‖J(u)−J(v)‖*.
relations.explanation: Summable decomposed increments converge as two monotone cone series, proving Banach completeness in actual Borel differences. A norm-Cauchy sequence of sources has bounded energy roots and is strongly Cauchy; completion produces its limiting potential, and curvature continuity identifies the source limit. This proves closed image, not arbitrary-data solvability.

links.label: Theorem 9.3 and proof: difference-series construction
Theorem 9.5: exact dual norm and curvature continuity
Theorem 9.6 and proof: close the source image

hypotheses: Keep one fixed strict Laurent geometry and background S.
Supply a completed reference potential v∈C and a finite constant M≥0 with 0≤μ≤M μ̂_v as Radon measures on every Borel set.
relations.explanation: Mixed Hölder proves literal integrability and the norm bound on every difference. Domination transfers the completed tester estimate to ∫|u_j−u| dμ, proving strong L¹ continuity. The fixed dominated interval is also weak-star compact and norm closed. This route supplies strong continuity but does not supply Ξ=0.

links.label: Fixed-source integrability lemma and proof
Fixed-domination theorem, especially FD7–FD8

hypotheses: Fix S and the strict Laurent geometry, and let μ be positive Radon, annihilate the relative null ideal, and define an absolutely integrable norm-bounded literal functional on all of D_S.
No fixed-source domination and no additional finite-total-mass assumption is available.
Missing: prove ∫|u_j−u| dμ→0 for every strongly convergent row in C, including a general nonzero limit; a qualified ordered-rooftop or finite-minorant estimate is a proposed route.
relations.explanation: ED-STRONG asks whether literal norm boundedness already implies the continuity needed for the variational datum. It is a separate unresolved route to the same condition supplied by fixed domination. Nonliteral dual counterexamples and varying-background estimates do not settle this fixed-background literal question.

hypotheses: Work on the same complete cone C with the established sharp midpoint estimate and completed energy continuity.
The datum belongs to the norm dual and is strongly continuous on C; literal positive data are the source-equation subclass used here.
relations.explanation: The dual norm bounds the energies of maximizing rows. The midpoint gap makes those rows strongly Cauchy. Completeness gives a limit, and strong continuity passes the datum term. First variations only along segments in C give the polar normal n; they do not assert arbitrary two-sided variations at the optimizer.

links.label: Theorem 9.9 and proof: maximize, then take cone variations
Proposition 7.6: midpoint estimate used in the proof

hypotheses: Use the normal pair u=Π(ℓ_μ), n=ℓ_μ−J(u) for the literal positive Radon datum in the fixed geometry.
For every original compact smooth φ, both ψ₀±ε_φφ are admissible, and the two probe integrals defining Ξ are finite.
Impose the additional equality Ξ=−n(ψ₀)=0.
relations.explanation: Testing the normal inequality in both probe directions gives |n(φ)|≤ε_φ⁻¹Ξ. Zero defect therefore kills every original scalar test error; literal integration and Radon uniqueness identify μ̂_u=μ. Variational uniqueness identifies every solution with u. The same theorem proves the converse: existence of a source solution forces Ξ=0, so zero defect and solvability are equivalent under these hypotheses.

links.label: Theorem 9.13 and proof: defect estimate and both directions
Proposition 9.12: the two admissible directions

hypotheses: Use the fixed q=1 two-dimensional torus background and a bounded actual admissible reference w<0, with finite total source mass, compact strict negative sublevels, canonical no loss, and all two-sided compact test directions.
The counterexample data are μ_j=f_jμ_w, with 1≤f_j≤3/2 and f_j→1 uniformly; they remain literal and strongly continuous.
relations.explanation: A source in the full completed cone would have a convex zero-boundary moment trace solving the prescribed real Poisson equation. The constructed Poisson solution is not convex, so no such source exists. The exact probe equivalence forces Ξ(μ_j)>0. This blocks the proposed inference from strong continuity, domination or smooth positive density to zero defect.

links.label: Fixed-source counterexample, FP15–FP19 and proof
Theorem 9.13: failure of solvability means positive defect

hypotheses: The zero-defect criterion is available after the variational optimizer is constructed.
Missing: hypotheses on the given measure, geometry and explicitly supplied reference objects that force both strong continuity and zero defect before assuming a solution.

For the proposed local inverse route, additionally establish the linearized range, a bounded right inverse with all boundary and harmonic-moment constraints, and preservation of that range by the nonlinear remainder.
relations.explanation: The exact compatibility criterion locates the remaining task but does not perform it. Existing finite-mode inverse constructions motivate a range-controlled route; smooth positive perturbations alone cannot be used as its hypothesis because the source-gap counterexample rules them out.

hypotheses: The remaining degree is q=1, in arbitrary ambient dimension, and the original smooth core has the stated faithful regular strongly local coercive part-form realization on V∩supp S.
The signed Radon datum has finite total variation and its total variation vanishes on energy-capacity polar Borel sets.
The solution uses the renormalized zero-boundary class: clipped membership in H, the scalar chain identity and the vanishing radiation tail.
relations.explanation: Approximate diffuse data by finite-energy nests, solve by the Riesz potential and pass the L¹ and clipping estimates to the transposition limit. The chain and radiation conditions identify every renormalized candidate with that limit. This is an independent linear theorem in H; it provides no implication that the solution lies in the nonlinear positive-potential cone C.

For classical representatives, supply actual regularization or relative detection linking the Borel capacity class to an ambient classical psh representative, together with its comparison and boundary properties.
relations.explanation: The existing proofs identify exactly where geometry controls truncation, integration by parts and loss at the boundary. Those are requirements for extension, not consequences of having a negative exhaustion alone. Recovering a classical representative is a second task: curvature quotients and capacity quotients cannot be identified without a theorem.

Problem 7.2: the missing representative theorem

hypotheses: Specify a first-energy class of Green currents satisfying Dg_Z+δ_Z=ω_Z and admissible truncations.
Missing: proper-intersection or replacement conditions controlling multiplication along cycles, coefficient integrability, and independence of presentations and truncations.
For curvature-generated expressions, separately prove the required relation descent and comparison with the existing smooth, formal and delta-form products.

Neither input alone defines products with cycle currents. The arrow marks the proposed interface to an open Green product theory, not an established implication.

links.label: Problem 7.4 and the algebraic/analytic division of work

hypotheses: Specify the adelic metrized line bundles and retain the geometric and boundary-completion hypotheses of the established continuous local Chern theory.
Missing locally: the chosen finite-energy intersection integral and its metric-change formula, with approximation independence.
Missing globally: a placewise summable dominating estimate, compatible boundary control and the product formula; global positivity retains its own geometric hypotheses.

Local measure positivity does not imply arithmetic nefness, and the Green-product project is not asserted to be a proved prerequisite or a sufficient route to this adelic goal.

links.label: Problem 7.5: finite-energy adelic intersection

The modification must belong to a mapping class in which the required current operations are already defined; retain the relative null ideal instead of identifying it with ambient polarity.

They supply a proposed starting point for singularity invariance, but invariance of nonpolar mass and transport through a modification still require their own stability proof. No arbitrary-current pullback is inferred.

hypotheses: Work on an original ordinary domain, with f=a−b bounded actual classical psh differences and an allowed positive separately closed tail Q of sub-top degree.
For Stieltjes curvature, the scalar function is finite convex on an interval containing the local range of f; its second derivative is used as a measure, including its atoms.

For uniform outer coarea, a and b are bounded on the same ordinary domain Ω, and Q=T_(S,q−1)(v₁,…,v_(q−1)) is a top-minus-one normalized mixed tail of the same S on Ω; use compact cutoffs, relative CLN estimates and bounded relative quasicontinuity.

Fubini and the scalar chain rule give coarea; the hinge representation of a convex function gives Stieltjes curvature with the strict/weak jump correction. Uniform trace bounds and relative quasicontinuity pass the fixed energy measures to an ordinary-open outer energy-capacity bound. hypotheses: Use the original strict Laurent domain and an extending allowed S, with q≥1 and its fixed zero-boundary barrier ρ.
The starting actual negative classical u has compact strict negative sublevels; no initial no-loss or finite-energy hypothesis is imposed on u.
Choose a prescribed compact H inside the domain and a positive matching tolerance; the construction glues to Aρ on a boundary collar.
relations.explanation: The attenuation v=−log(1−u) transforms the basic capacity-tail estimate into an exponential tail and hence gives no loss. Gluing v minus the tolerance to a large barrier preserves its exact pole set, supplies finite total boundary mass, and converts the exponential tail into every positive power energy. These are representatives for specified complete pole sets, not a characterization of all polar sets.

links.label: LP1–LP6: logarithmic attenuation produces no loss
LP7–LP10: all-power representatives and exponential tails

hypotheses: Use the exact original q-dimensional polydisc background S=[V] and its Gauss shell calibration, with q≥1.
For the continuity example fix s>0 and set u_T=T^(−s/(q+s))g_T, so e_s(u_T)=1.
For the recursive example take the unbounded logarithmic pole u=log max_i|T_i|; its lower multipliers are coefficient-integrable, but it has persistent truncation loss.
relations.explanation: The scaled shell has critical weighted mass exactly one at σ(T), while local truncated gap capacities tend to zero; this leaves a Dirac limit at the origin. For the logarithmic pole, bounded uncut top products tend to the same Dirac mass but every nonpolar restriction removes it. These constructions disprove the proposed weaker hypotheses; they do not contradict strong critical continuity, strict subcritical continuity, or the no-loss recursion.

panels.title: From truncation to a complete energy space
panels.summary: The proof uses capacity-tail control and global Green exchange together. Strong Cauchy control supplies the extra uniform tails needed at critical degree, and completion then closes the source image.

panels.title: When a projection solves the source equation
panels.summary: Fixed domination proves the datum-continuity condition; the general literal-dual route remains open. Projection, the two-sided probe and zero defect must be combined to solve the equation. The counterexample blocks any shortcut from strong continuity to zero defect.

panels.title: The linear branch and open extensions
panels.summary: The q=1 Dirichlet theorem closes in its own part-energy space. Domain/representative, singularity, Green-product and adelic extensions each require a different missing interface; none is displayed as an automatic consequence of the energy theorem.

panels.title: Scalar levels, pole representatives and critical limits
panels.summary: The chain rule creates level and Stieltjes calculus; capacity tails create all-power representatives of specified poles. Exact radial shells independently explain why the critical hypotheses cannot be weakened.

panels.title: Relative envelopes, variational constraints and failed shortcuts
panels.summary: Strong completion supports Perron and constrained variational constructions. The same framework identifies the sharp rooftop obstruction and separates Banach duals, literal data and weak compactness.

panels.title: Explicit parameter and radial source inverses
panels.summary: Two specified model mechanisms solve compatible source data. The parameter tester capacity has its own exact formula; a countable-probe counterexample shows why it cannot replace the full capacity.

panels.title: Clamped source graphs, interfaces and the extension problem
panels.summary: A complemented linear range feeds a controlled nonlinear graph. Boundary traces generate a separate interface measure; moving interfaces expose topology and ideal limits, while extension to new backgrounds remains an open step.
